name: United Kingdom
notes: You can’t transit airside to Ireland or anywhere else in the Common Travel Area. An immigration officer at the UK border decides whether you can transit without a visa.

exemptions: A valid visa for Australia, Canada, New Zealand or the USA, whether or not you’re travelling to or from there
A visa for Australia, Canada, New Zealand or the USA, when you’re on a reasonable journey from that country and last entered it with the visa less than 6 months ago
A valid permanent residence permit from Australia, Canada (issued after 28 June 2002), New Zealand or the USA (issued after 21 April 1998, or the other US documents the Home Office lists)
A valid residence permit in the common format issued by an EEA country or Switzerland, or a valid category D visa for one
A valid Irish biometric visa endorsed BC or BC BIVS, when going on to a destination outside Ireland and the Common Travel Area
A UK Standard Visitor visa, Marriage Visitor visa or EU Settlement Scheme family permit
conditions: Have a confirmed onward flight leaving the same day from the same airport
Hold the documents your final destination requires (for example its visa)
rules.notes: If you’re exempt, you can transit airside without a visa when you meet the conditions. Otherwise apply for a Direct Airside Transit Visa: it costs £41.50 and a decision usually takes 3 weeks.

conditions: Have a confirmed onward flight leaving the same day from the same airport
Hold the documents your final destination requires (for example its visa)
rules.notes: Your passport needs a UK visa only to pass through border control (for example to change airport or collect bags), not to change planes airside.
Your passport isn’t on the UK’s visa lists, and you don’t need an ETA to change planes without passing through border control. You need one to pass through border control.

name: Schengen Area
notes: An airport transit visa covers only the international transit area. Leaving it means entering the Schengen Area, which needs the documents in the entry rule.

exemptions: A valid Schengen visa, national long-stay visa or residence permit issued by a Schengen country

A valid residence permit from an EU country that doesn’t fully apply the Schengen rules, or one of the residence permits from Andorra, Canada, Japan, San Marino or the United States listed in Annex V of the Visa Code

A valid visa for an EU country that doesn’t fully apply the Schengen rules, or for Canada, Japan or the United States, when travelling to that country or another non-EU country, or returning from it after using the visa
Family members of EU citizens covered by the Visa Code
Holders of diplomatic passports
rules.notes: Belgium, Spain, the Netherlands and Switzerland don’t apply it to service or special passports. The Netherlands also exempts seafarers with a valid seafarer’s identity document.
